newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bomb jitters spoil Purim holiday in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Bomb jitters spoil Purim holiday in Israel.

text.p: The bang from seven-year-old Yotam Yaacobi's cap pistol made jittery Israelis jump and mumble curses at a Purim holiday street carnival on Sunday in a city still reeling from an Arab suicide bombing.
"I'm doing it because I know it makes them nervous," said the spunky boy in a ninja costume. "They are nervous because an Arab killed Israelis."

Police with dogs stood at every intersection along Tel Aviv's fashionable Dizengoff street, closed to traffic for the carnival on the holiday commemorating the Jews' salvation from genocide in ancient Persia. Hundreds of police were on patrol.
On Friday, an Arab suicide bomber killed three Israeli women in a crowded Tel Aviv cafe near Dizengoff, where newspaper stands on Sunday displayed banner headlines reading "The terror is back".
The militant Moslem group Hamas has threatened more attacks.

Purim, one of the most joyous holidays on the Jewish calendar, usually draws thousands of families in costume to Dizengoff. On Sunday, only handfuls of people watched jugglers and dancers perform on stages scattered along the street.
Tel Aviv Mayor Roni Milo looked on the bright side.
"Even the awful terrorism and the pain we all have are not stopping the activity in this city. I am happy we are still a city that never stops," he told reporters.

In the Dizengoff centre shopping mall, near the spot where a suicide bomber killed 13 people on Purim a year ago, Sara Shlomo paused to look at a newspaper photo of a baby girl wounded in Friday's blast.
The baby's mother and the two other women who died in Friday's attack were to be buried later on Sunday.

"The picture is frightening. But where can you go with two children on Purim?" Shlomo said, glancing at her two sons, aged two and eight months, dressed as a bunny and an alien. "I spent two weeks making their costumes. We just couldn't stay at home."

Outside the Apropo cafe, due to reopen on Sunday after the funerals, workers repaired spotlights on palm trees in the courtyard where the suicide bomber, a West Bank Palestinian, sat at a table and blew himself up.
Memorial candles flickered in a cardboard box covered with red carnations on the sidewalk.
"No matter how many times this happens -- and it has happened a lot in Tel Aviv -- you never get used to it," said Motti Sasson, arguing politics with other men at the site.
Sasson said he lived two blocks from the cafe and saw the carnage, two years after he witnessed the suicide bombing of a bus on Dizengoff street in which 22 people were killed.
Upstairs in the cafe, psychologists met with some 40 staff members for a group therapy session aimed at easing their anxiety before getting back to work.
"I had nightmares all Friday night. I kept seeing pictures of the explosion in my mind," one waiter said.
